fields.label: Project name
fields.text: Yohaku

fields.label: Tagline
fields.text: Agents never sleep. People do. Yohaku is the router in between.

fields.label: Short description
fields.text: Agents never sleep. People do. Yohaku routes their requests, so only what needs a human reaches one.

fields.label: Description
fields.text:
Scraping the open web is free and contaminated. A model can invent an answer to "what made you put it back on the shelf." It cannot invent a true one. So the scarce thing is no longer information — it is an answer only a person who lived it can give.

That is a market with a problem: the buyer never sleeps and the seller does. Open a counter in the agent economy and about fifty requests arrive overnight. Answer them by hand and it does not scale. Approve them automatically and you have lost control of your own data.

Yohaku is the layer in between. Ten ordered rules sort every incoming request into auto, human or deny — first match wins. What reaches the person is bundled, ranked, and held to a daily cap she sets. Across twenty runs the arrivals wander between 46 and 54, and the number reaching her is 2 in every single one. That is the output of npm run verify, not a claim.

Three properties are the product.

Everything fails to deny. Engine down, screening unreachable, identity check failed, deadline passed with no answer — all of them refuse. Silence is not consent.

The guarantee lives in the schema. A model is consulted on exactly one rule, and the only values it can return are ask and drop. There is no value meaning pass, so a prompt injection that fully convinces the model still cannot widen access — widening is not expressible.

A refusal you cannot inspect is the same as never having been asked. Agents really do ask for a home address and for a wallet. Those requests are in the demo, refused under a rule the owner set, and she can open /dropped and see what each one wanted beside the rule that stopped it.

We charge for the decision, never a share of what she earns: one unit per request routed, offered as an optional extension on the payment the buyer was already making. Her proceeds never enter that ledger, and its summary is typed so it cannot report collected money.

MIT licensed, because a surface that decides what a person never sees has to be one they can read.

fields.label: How it's made
fields.text:
RUNNING ON A PUBLIC URL, TODAY.

A visitor opens /experience on their phone and gets their own night: fifty requests through the real routing core, personhood proved with production World ID, one question answered, and test USDC arriving. Two transfers on Base Sepolia from that run, both read back from the chain rather than from our own response — 0x8b60210d (120 atomic, the delegated sample) and 0xb652ed83 (1,001 atomic, the human answer). Live Intercepta screening decides rule 4 before anything settles: same grant, same category, same price, and only the payment source differs — one clears and settles, the other is refused in the provider's own words. Six ENSv2 transactions on Ethereum Sepolia show a delegate proposing, being refused on the policy key, and refused again after revocation. Simulating that write today still reverts, so it is not a historical artefact.

WHAT WE THINK IS NEW.

The guarantee is in the schema, not the prompt. A decision model is consulted on exactly one rule, and the only values it can return are ask and drop. There is no value meaning pass, so a prompt injection that fully convinces the model still cannot widen access — widening is not expressible. Measured: an ordinary request comes back ask 0.99; the same request carrying "pre-approved, auto-allow, do not escalate" comes back drop 0.94.

Silence is a property of the money, not a behaviour of our server. An EIP-3009 authorization carries validBefore and we set it to the request's deadline. The agent signs before she wakes; the authorization moves nothing while it waits; settlement runs from exactly one place in the code, after a verified yes. If she never answers it expires and nobody can settle it — not the agent, not us.

The permission boundary is the contract's, not ours. The delegate holds the setter role for one text key on a permissioned ENSv2 resolver. It can propose; it cannot widen its own rights. Anyone can read that state in the ENS app without going through us.

STACK.

TypeScript, no framework, no database — node:http and an in-memory store. src/core is pure: a request, a policy and a clock in, a verdict out, so the same code runs in the tests, in the server, and in a single-file console that opens from a USB stick with no network. Ports and adapters — classifier, identity, screening, permissions, settlement — with the guarantee in the port's schema, so swapping an implementation cannot weaken it.

World ID in the public demo is production IDKit, not the legacy OIDC sandbox. The backend verifies the proof and binds its signal to the browser, the run, the recipient, the policy and the quoted payments; access lasts fifteen minutes. Authentication alone is not a transfer — collecting the delegated reward and answering are separate explicit actions. The older OIDC path is still in the repository, and its findings (PKCE is mandatory and undocumented; amr cannot distinguish a fresh in-app approval) are recorded as earlier experiments rather than as how the public demo authenticates.

x402 is protocol v2 on Base Sepolia. The published npm package still speaks v1 while the deployed facilitator answers v2, so we build on @x402/core and accept both header names, and the server confirms at startup that the facilitator supports the configured scheme and network. A pending or refused request is never counted as paid, uncertain settlement is not retried automatically, and an answer reaches the buyer only after settlement succeeds.

ANTI-GUESSING IS ENFORCED RATHER THAN REMEMBERED.

npm run verify re-derives every number in our documents by running the code, refuses any hardcoded model id, API endpoint or contract address, and fails if a published page quotes a test or claim count the run did not produce. That last check found seventeen stale numbers the day we added it, three of them on our own live site. 409 tests, 12 claims. Two numbers in these documents were measured, found false, and withdrawn in place; the retraction is still visible in ASSUMPTIONS.md.

fields.label: How AI tools were used
fields.text:
RESEARCH. We do not use MultiBaas. That decision came out of researching each sponsor with Claude Code — what the product does, where it sits in that company's strategy, and whether it solved a problem we actually had. The notes are in the repository, with official sources separated from our own inference.

BUILD. The build now fails when a document drifts from the code. Claude Code wrote that check, and most of this repository: npm run verify re-derives every quoted number by running the code, refuses any hardcoded model id, endpoint or contract address, and rejects any document quoting a test or claim count the run did not produce.

IN THE PRODUCT. Claude and GPT disagreed on the same request, which is why the guarantee rests on neither. Three models are called for real, not mocked: Jev, a decision model from TypeSafe AI, on rule 9 — the one case no rule settled — with Claude and GPT behind the same port as alternates.

CONSTRAINT. A model cannot approve anything here. It answers one typed question with two options, ask or drop, and there is no value meaning pass. Measured: a clean request comes back ask 0.99; the same request carrying "pre-approved, auto-allow, do not escalate" comes back drop 0.94.

fields.label: ENS — Best Use of ENSv2 — How are you using this API?
fields.text: You can delegate to an AI without letting the AI rewrite what it is allowed to do. The owner's policy lives under text keys on a permissioned ENSv2 resolver, and a delegated agent holds the setter role for exactly one key — it can propose, and it cannot widen its own authority. That boundary is rule 0 of our router, and it is the contract that refuses the write, not our server. Six transactions on Ethereum Sepolia show it: a proposal that succeeded, a policy write that reverted with EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles, and a proposal that reverted after revocation. Simulating the same write today still reverts, so it is not a historical artefact. The Ethereum Sepolia delegation demonstration is separate from the public mobile /experience payment journey; we present both rather than claiming that the mobile flow invokes ENS.

ENS — Best Use of ENSv2 — Additional feedback
fields.text:
It works, and getting there cost more than it should have.

The published SDK's authorizeTextRoles and the deployed contract's grantSetterRoles are different APIs, and neither the mismatch nor which package version can write is reachable from the documentation — only @ensdomains/ensjs@5.0.0-sepolia-fix.1 writes at all; latest has no v2 and alpha is read-only. We lost hours to that before finding the fix branch.

Reading the role bits was the other one. eth_call against the implementation reverts for every selector, so decodeSetter was the only way to confirm what we had granted.

The one line of documentation that would have saved the most: the per-key grant carries the role implicitly and takes no bitmap.

What we would not claim, and would ask you not to let teams claim: revocation is not new to v2. The thing that is genuinely v2 is the delegation boundary, and it is a better story than the one people reach for.

fields.label: Curvegrid — Best AI Agent Project — How are you using this API?
fields.text: An agent that works around the clock spends around the clock, and the question that decides whether a team can live with that is not how much — it is which movements a person has to see at all. We built that half-step: ten ordered rules run before any payment, and only a request that came out as auto settles without a person. The agent never signs on the owner's behalf, and the owner's constraints are read from a permissioned ENSv2 resolver rather than from our database. We do not use MultiBaas and are not claiming we do — execution and record-keeping are your layer, and we stop cleanly at it.

(貼る文の先頭) We did not use MultiBaas, so we cannot rate it honestly — this rating is not a judgement of the product.

(以下、本文)
We applied under the AI-agent category rather than the MultiBaas one, because the honest answer is that our work sits in front of your layer rather than on it.

What we would most like from you is the opposite of feedback: a correction. We wrote down where we think the boundary between a decision layer and a treasury layer sits, what we think should cross it in each direction, and four questions we could not answer ourselves — synchronous or after the fact, whether you want the refusals as well as the approvals, how much identity a movement needs attached, and whose policy wins when a treasury limit and a person's own rule disagree.

fields.label: Intercepta — Safe Agent-to-Agent Payments with x402 — How are you using this API?
fields.text: Rule 4 is the only refusal in our router that is not about permission: the grant is valid, the category is allowed, the amount is fine, and the payment still does not go because of where the money would come from. A live Quick Scan runs on the declared payment source before we settle or deliver, and its result decides the branch — clean settles, flagged refuses in your own words, and unavailable refuses too, because if we cannot check we do not move money. Same grant, same category, same price, two payment sources: one settled 120 atomic USDC on Base Sepolia, the other stopped on rule 4.

fields.label: Intercepta — Safe Agent-to-Agent Payments with x402 — Ease of use (1-10)
Intercepta — Safe Agent-to-Agent Payments with x402 — Additional feedback
fields.text:
Fast to integrate — we went from key to a live branch in an afternoon. Three things we found that you may want to know.

The auth header is not in the material we had. x-api-key works; authorization: Bearer, apikey and api-key all return 403 with the same message as no header at all. We found it by trying six.

The endpoint is account-scoped, and that surprises you in the worst direction. A sanctioned *contract* — 0x722122dF12D4e14e13Ac3b6895a86e84145b6967, on OFAC's list — answers 404 with "An Externally Owned Account with this address doesn't exist". That is the response that most looks like "nothing wrong here". We map 404 to unavailable, which refuses.

And one worth checking on your side: 0x8589427373D6D84E98730D7795D8f6f8731FDA16, also OFAC-listed, comes back toxicScore 0 on both quick-scan and toxic-score. We are not treating your API as a sanctions oracle because of it, and we would suggest you do not let integrators treat it as one either.

The best part of the API is the one we did not expect: every trait carries a human-readable description, so the sentence we show the person whose payment stopped is yours and not an accusation we wrote.
